title: Stanford Has a Secret Course That Teaches 12 People How to Extract Value From Other Humans
dek: The course never appears in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The students lie, the author says, not by accident but because the machine has rewarded it for years.
why: This is not a generic Silicon Valley critique — it is a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and named people; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.
who: Founders and engineers doing early-stage investing, hiring new grads, or watching the AI bubble and Silicon Valley's talent pipeline.
skip: 0:00–1:01 and 20:33–22:38 are show promos and ad breaks; skip them.

points.h: You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
points.body: Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just showed up hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "when you start a company someday, come back to us" — and otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't actually believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one overnight sensation. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that nobody follows up: you can lie and face no consequences.

points.h: The secret course teaches extracting value
points.body: Stanford has a course that never appears in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who has packaged himself as a professor. It admits only 12 students a year, and merely knowing it exists is a status marker. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong flavor of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she went on to raise millions, drop out of Stanford, and this despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she released a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley cheered her on anyway, installed her in a mansion, and invited her back to Stanford to speak.

points.h: Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
points.body: During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor presented the case of a software defect that killed four people in a radiotherapy device, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense that these people felt any need to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest at the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

points.h: The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
points.body: Board members who removed Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of their heaviest reasons was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence that Tessier-Lavigne himself falsified data: the problem lay in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated results in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

points.h: Four days after being ousted, the mansion closed
points.body: Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him about it, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you could imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

points.h: Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
points.body: Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface like ducks, making everything look effortless, while underneath their legs paddle furiously just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — captain of the women's soccer team, an NCAA champion, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just led held a mental health night and never mentioned her name.

points.h: A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
points.body: Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to move a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities profiting from patents; in its final valid year that patent accounted for 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year, Theo found that Cohen had been found liable for fraud by a court: he had pitched investors on a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, saying it was already approved to treat another condition, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed.

points.h: Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is the signal
points.body: The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than landing an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the reality. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who is still standing when the music stops and who is left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long; it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

Stanford's campus hackathon, a weekend project competition that investors treat as a high-signal zone.
A term Stanford coined: gliding elegantly on the surface while paddling furiously underneath.
In the source, people who start companies only because others are doing it, without real ability.
